cards.explanation: The word is steady. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends (Job 2:11), says, “Your words have steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). He adds that Job braced knees that were buckling. So Job was the one folks leaned on when their legs went wobbly, friends, and that's a great thing to be known for.

The answer is his confidence and hope. Eliphaz asks, “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” (Job 4:6). He's pointing Job back to his own reverence and his upright ways. Notice it's phrased as a question, so Eliphaz is nudging Job to lean on them.

The answer is whether the innocent ever perish. Eliphaz pleads, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). He's asking Job to think about whether he's ever seen that happen. Eliphaz is making his case, bakers, and it's the question his whole speech leans on.

The word is reap. Eliphaz says, “As I have observed, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.” (Job 4:8). It's a farming picture: what you plant is what comes up. Eliphaz says he observed this himself, and I think he's counting on Job to nod along.

The answer is the breath of God. Eliphaz says, “By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.” (Job 4:9). He's talking about those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, who he says reap the same (Job 4:8). Those are his words, friends, so we hear them as his claim.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “The lion may roar, and the fierce lion may growl, yet the teeth of the young lions are broken.” (Job 4:10). The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered (Job 4:11). That's a lot of noise for a sad ending.
The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “…fear and trembling came over me and made all my bones shudder.” (Job 4:14). There's no peace in that sentence, friends. Even his bones were in on the shaking.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says it “…stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form loomed before my eyes…” (Job 4:16). He saw a form, but he couldn't tell what it looked like. Then came a whispering voice.

The answer is whether a mortal can be more righteous than God. The voice asks, “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (Job 4:17). Eliphaz says it came in disquieting visions in the night, as a whispering voice. That's what he reports hearing.

The point is that people fall even shorter than angels. The voice says, “If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay…” (Job 4:18-19). It's a step-up argument: if that's said of angels, then how much more of people. The voice is stacking the comparison against people.

The answer is True. The voice says, “They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever.” (Job 4:20). The word “unnoticed” is right there. It's a heavy line, friends, and I think it's worth letting it sit for a second.
The answer is False. Eliphaz says the fool's sons “…are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender.” (Job 5:4). Nobody stands up for them in that courtroom. It's a lonely scene.

The answer is that the hungry consume it. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.” (Job 5:5). They take it even from the thorns. That's the picture he paints of the cursed fool.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground.” (Job 5:6). So trouble doesn't come up like a seedling, bakers. It's a short verse, but it sets up what he says next.

The answer is that he would bring his cause before God. Eliphaz says, “However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him…” (Job 5:8). That's what he says he'd do in Job's place. Then he goes on to talk about the One who does great and unsearchable things (Job 5:9).
The word is lowly. Eliphaz says, “He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety.” (Job 5:11). The ones who were down get lifted up. That's good news for anyone who's felt low.

The word is corrects. Eliphaz says, “Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.” (Job 5:17). He tells Job not to despise that discipline. Correction isn't fun, friends, but Eliphaz calls the man who receives it blessed.

The answer is True. Eliphaz says, “For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.” (Job 5:18). Both halves are in the same verse. The wounding and striking come first, and then the binding and healing.

The answer is that Job will laugh at them. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.” (Job 5:22). That's quite a promise to make to a man who has lost so much (Job 1:13-19). Whatever you think of Eliphaz's words, the laughing is what he says.

The answer is False. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.” (Job 5:25). Like the grass of the earth means a lot of them. Eliphaz is painting a full house, friends.

The answer is in full vigor. Eliphaz says, “You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.” (Job 5:26). Grain gathered in season is ripe and ready. That's the picture he gives Job.
